title: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Business Tempo
shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Business Tempo
summary: This sub-technique covers collection about when a victim organisation is active and when it is not: operational hours, working days, holiday shutdowns, and the timing of purchases and shipments. Business tempo is a scheduling input rather than a targeting input, and it is what turns otherwise generic activity into a well-timed operation. Adversaries derive it from published opening hours and holiday notices, social media activity patterns, event and travel announcements, procurement schedules, and shipment tracking data that shows when new equipment arrives. The operational payoff is choosing a window with the fewest watchers, sending messages when staff are distracted, and aligning delivery of malicious or tainted components with real orders. Detection is behavioural and depends on baselining: authentication, virtual private network, and administrative activity outside established hours, or first-time logins from unfamiliar locations on weekends, only stand out when normal tempo is measured. That makes time-of-day baselining one of the few reliable controls for this otherwise invisible activity.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique is about learning when an organisation is busy and when it is quiet. It covers working hours, quiet days, and the timing of purchases. Attackers use this knowledge to choose the best moment to act.
beginner.whyItMatters: A message sent during a busy Monday morning is easy to miss. An intrusion on a quiet holiday weekend may go unnoticed for much longer. Attackers want the window with the fewest people watching. If your alerts only reach a person during office hours, that window is very wide.
howItWorks: The attacker notes the opening hours and public holidays shown on your website.
They watch social media for quiet periods, such as shutdowns or team offsites.
They study when your staff post, because activity often follows working hours.
They look for purchase and shipment dates that show when new equipment arrives.
They choose a moment when few people are at their desks to send a message.
They may aim at long weekends, when monitoring and response are thinnest.
beginner.example: Imagine you need to call a large office about a bill. You want a person who can actually help you. So you check the website for opening hours. You notice the office closes early on Fridays and shuts completely for a week in summer. You call on a Tuesday morning, when the team is at full strength. Attackers use the same information in the opposite way. They look for the quiet Friday or the holiday week. They want the moment when the fewest people are watching the screens. Business tempo gathering is simply learning that calendar.
takeaways: Know your own quiet hours, because attackers plan their activity around them.
Make sure alerts reach a real person outside office hours and on public holidays.
Public calendars and social posts tell outsiders when your teams are away.

objectives: Define business tempo and explain why timing informs adversary decision making.
Identify public sources that reveal working hours, shutdowns, and holiday periods.
Explain how purchase and shipment timing relates to supply chain activity.
Describe how time-of-day baselining helps detect activity outside normal tempo.
Recommend monitoring coverage that remains effective during quiet periods.
